To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the identifiability criterion is a simple generalization of the criterion of Pearl (1993), and (2) the sufficient criterion is a generalization of the sufficient criterion of Pearl (2000).

(1) a causal effect of a singleton variable is identifiable if and only if the effect can be written as a linear function of the observed data, and if and only if it is invariant to any intervention that is compatible with the causal graph; (2) if a causal effect is not identifiable then it is not invariant to any intervention; and (3) if a causal graph is acyclic then the causal effect of any variable on any set is identifiable if and ony if it is invariant

(i) the identification of a causal effect requires that all variables in the model be either: (a) observed; or (b) exogenous, and (ii), if the effect is identified, then the causal graph must satisfy a condition that we call "causal sufficiency".
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of causal effects in the presence of unobserved variables
the identification of the causal effects from nonexperimental data, with the use of a directed acyclical graph to represent the assumptions about the causal structure of the model.
the assessment of the consequences of policy actions from nonexperimental data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the effects of a single variable on any set are identifiable if and only if the effects of that variable on all variables are identifiable, and that the effects of any set of variables on any subset of variables are identifiable if the effects of any variable on the subset are identifiable.

the effects of the action on the set of variables are not identifiable if and only if there is a set of unobserved variables, such that, if the action were to affect one of them, it would affect the others as well.
the effects of a variable are identifiable if and only if the variable is a descendant of all the variables on which it is assumed to have an effect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in order for the causal effects of any singleton variable on any other variable to be identifiable, there must be a path from that variable to every other variable in the graph, and the graph must be acyclic.
the identifiability criterion is that all paths from the variable of interest to any variable of interest must be blocked by an unobserved confounder.
the causal effects of any variable on any set are identifiable from the observed data if and only if the variable is a collider in the causal graph.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the identifiability conditions for a model are determined by the structure of the graph, not by the values of the model parameters.

a general identification condition for all the causal effects of one variable can be expressed in terms of a set of simple and intuitive conditions, which can be easily checked in the context of a given causal graph and set of assumptions.
, under certain circumstances, a causal effect is identifiable from nonexperimental data, if and only if the effect can be measured in a randomized experiment.
